        "text": "Suppose $\\left|w_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|w_{d}\\right\\rangle$ is a basis set for some vector space $V$ with an inner product.\nThere is a useful method, the Gram-Schmidt procedure, which can be used to produce an orthonormal basis set $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{d}\\right\\rangle$ for the vector space $V$.\nDefine $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv\\left|w_{1}\\right\\rangle / \\|\\left|w_{1}\\right\\rangle \\|$, and for $1 \\leq k \\leq d-1$ define $\\left|v_{k+1}\\right\\rangle$ inductively by\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n\\left|v_{k+1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{\\left|w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle-\\sum_{i=1}^{k}\\left\\langle v_{i} \\mid w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle}{\\|\\left|w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle-\\sum_{i=1}^{k}\\left\\langle v_{i} \\mid w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle \\|} \\tag{2.17}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\n"

        "end": 396,
        "text": "With these conventions, the inner product on a Hilbert space can be given a convenient matrix representation.\nLet $|w\\rangle=\\sum_{i} w_{i}|i\\rangle$ and $|v\\rangle=\\sum_{j} v_{j}|j\\rangle$ be representations of vectors $|w\\rangle$ and $|v\\rangle$ with respect to some orthonormal basis $|i\\rangle$.\nThen, since $\\langle i \\mid j\\rangle=\\delta_{i j}$,\n\n$$\n\\begin{align*}\n\\langle v \\mid w\\rangle & =\\left(\\sum_{i} v_{i}|i\\rangle, \\sum_{j} w_{j}|j\\rangle\\right)=\\sum_{i j} v_{i}^{*} w_{j} \\delta_{i j}=\\sum_{i} v_{i}^{*} w_{i}  \\tag{2.18}\\\\\n& =\\left[v_{1}^{*} \\ldots v_{n}^{*}\\right]\\left[\\begin{array}{c}\nw_{1} \\\\\n\\vdots \\\\\nw_{n}\n\\end{array}\\right] \\tag{2.19}\n\\end{align*}\n$$\n\nThat is, the inner product of two vectors is equal to the vector inner product between two matrix representations of those vectors, provided the representations are written with respect to the same orthonormal basis.\nWe also see that the dual vector $\\langle v|$ has a nice interpretation as the row vector whose components are complex conjugates of the corresponding components of the column vector representation of $|v\\rangle$.\n"

        "text": "There is a useful way of representing linear operators which makes use of the inner product, known as the outer product representation.\nSuppose $|v\\rangle$ is a vector in an inner product space $V$, and $|w\\rangle$ is a vector in an inner product space $W$.\nDefine $|w\\rangle\\langle v|$ to be the linear operator from $V$ to $W$ whose action is defined by\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n(|w\\rangle\\langle v|)\\left(\\left|v^{\\prime}\\right\\rangle\\right) \\equiv|w\\rangle\\left\\langle v \\mid v^{\\prime}\\right\\rangle=\\left\\langle v \\mid v^{\\prime}\\right\\rangle|w\\rangle \\tag{2.20}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nThis equation fits beautifully into our notational conventions, according to which the expression $|w\\rangle\\left\\langle v \\mid v^{\\prime}\\right\\rangle$ could potentially have one of two meanings: we will use it to denote the result when the operator $|w\\rangle\\langle v|$ acts on $\\left|v^{\\prime}\\right\\rangle$, and it has an existing interpretation as the result of multiplying $|w\\rangle$ by the complex number $\\left\\langle v \\mid v^{\\prime}\\right\\rangle$.\nOur definitions are chosen so that these two potential meanings coincide.\nIndeed, we define the former in terms of the latter!\n"
